subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the AQA spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE AQA Chemistry simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Crude oil is best described as:
options: A finite mixture of hydrocarbons formed from ancient plankton
A mixture of metals and salts
A renewable resource made from living plants
questions.explain: Crude oil is a finite (non-renewable) mixture of hydrocarbons formed over millions of years from the remains of plankton.

questions.q: A hydrocarbon is a compound containing:
questions.explain: A hydrocarbon contains only hydrogen and carbon atoms. Most crude oil hydrocarbons are alkanes.

questions.q: What is the general formula for the alkanes?
questions.explain: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CnH2n+2, e.g. methane CH4, ethane C2H6.

questions.q: How many hydrogen atoms are in a molecule of propane (C3H?)?
questions.explain: Using CnH2n+2 with n=3: H = (2 x 3) + 2 = 8, so propane is C3H8.

questions.q: Fractional distillation separates crude oil based on differences in:
questions.explain: Fractions are separated by their different boiling points, which depend on molecular size (number of carbon atoms).

questions.q: In a fractionating column, where are the fractions with the smallest molecules collected?
options: Near the top, where it is coolest
They are not collected at all
Near the bottom, where it is hottest
questions.explain: Small molecules have low boiling points, so they rise highest before condensing and are collected at the cooler top of the column.

questions.q: As hydrocarbon molecules get larger, they generally become:
options: More viscous, less volatile and less flammable
Lighter in colour and less viscous
More volatile and easier to ignite
questions.explain: Larger hydrocarbons have higher boiling points, are more viscous, less volatile and burn less easily (less flammable).

questions.q: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon produces:
questions.explain: With plenty of oxygen, complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water and releases energy.

questions.q: Why is carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion dangerous?
options: It is explosive at all concentrations
It is highly acidic and burns the skin
It is a toxic, colourless, odourless gas that reduces oxygen transport in the blood
questions.explain: Carbon monoxide is toxic because it binds to haemoglobin, and it is colourless and odourless so it is hard to detect.

questions.q: Cracking is the process of:
options: Breaking large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones
Separating crude oil by boiling point
Removing all hydrogen from a molecule
Joining small molecules into large ones
questions.explain: Cracking breaks long-chain alkanes into shorter, more useful alkanes and alkenes using heat and a catalyst (or steam).

questions.q: Why is cracking economically important?
options: It removes the need for crude oil
It converts less useful long-chain fractions into shorter chains in higher demand, and makes alkenes for polymers
questions.explain: Cracking turns surplus long-chain molecules into shorter, in-demand fuels and produces alkenes used to make polymers.

questions.q: Alkenes are described as unsaturated because they contain:
questions.explain: Alkenes have at least one C=C double bond, making them unsaturated and more reactive than alkanes. General formula CnH2n.

questions.q: Which test distinguishes an alkene from an alkane?
options: Bromine water turns from orange to colourless with an alkene
A lit splint gives a squeaky pop with an alkene
Limewater turns cloudy with an alkene
Damp litmus paper is bleached by an alkane
questions.explain: Alkenes decolourise bromine water (orange to colourless) because bromine adds across the C=C bond; alkanes do not.

questions.q: When ethene reacts with steam in the presence of a catalyst, the product is:
questions.explain: Ethene + steam (with a phosphoric acid catalyst) undergoes hydration to form ethanol: C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH.

questions.q: Which functional group do all alcohols contain?
questions.explain: Alcohols contain the -OH functional group, e.g. ethanol C2H5OH. The homologous series includes methanol, ethanol, propanol, butanol.

questions.q: Which functional group is present in all carboxylic acids?
questions.explain: Carboxylic acids contain the -COOH group, e.g. ethanoic acid CH3COOH. They are weak acids that partially ionise in water.

questions.q: When ethanol is oxidised (for example by fermentation left open to air), it can form:
questions.explain: Oxidation of ethanol produces ethanoic acid, which is why wine left open turns sour (vinegar contains ethanoic acid).

questions.q: During addition polymerisation of alkene monomers:
options: The C=C double bonds open and monomers join with no other product formed
The polymer is smaller than the monomers
Water is released as a by-product
Two different monomers are always needed
questions.explain: In addition polymerisation the C=C double bonds open and many monomers join into a long chain; no other product is made.

questions.q: The polymer made from ethene monomers is called:
questions.explain: Ethene monomers polymerise to form poly(ethene), commonly known as polythene.

questions.q: How does condensation polymerisation differ from addition polymerisation?
options: It joins monomers with two functional groups and releases a small molecule such as water
It requires a C=C double bond only
It uses only one monomer and makes no by-product
questions.explain: Condensation polymerisation involves monomers with two functional groups and releases a small molecule (e.g. water) for each bond formed.
